name: Advanced Grammar: Units 1–3
description: Present and past at C1 level, unit by unit after *Advanced Grammar in Use* (4th ed.): own explanations and exercises.

blocks.text: State verbs usually take the present simple. A few of them (**attract**, **like**, **look**, **love**, **sound**) can take the present continuous when we want to stress that a situation is **temporary** or limited to the time around now.

items.text: I **love** living by the sea. *(always true for me)*
I**’m loving** the quiet now that the tourists have gone. *(for the moment)*

blocks.text: Some state verbs are hardly ever used in the continuous:

blocks.label: B
blocks.title: Two meanings: a state or an action

blocks.text: Some verbs describe a **state** with one meaning and an **action** with another. With the state meaning they take the present simple; with the action meaning they can take either form, depending on the context.

items.text: This parcel **weighs** three kilos. *(state: its weight)*
The nurse **is weighing** the baby. *(action: putting it on the scales)*
She **has** two older brothers. *(state: possession)*
She**’s having** a shower — can she call you back? *(action)*

blocks.text: Also: **appear**, **expect**, **feel**, **fit**, **have**, **imagine**, **look**, **measure**, **see**, **taste**, **think**, **weigh**.
With some verbs of thinking (**find**, **realise**, **regret**, **think**, **understand**) the present continuous shows that the thought has only just begun, or that we are not yet sure about it.

items.text: I **regret** agreeing to it. *(my view is settled)*
I**’m** already **regretting** agreeing to it. *(the feeling is growing)*

blocks.text: **Consider** meaning ‘think carefully about’ is usually continuous. **Agree**, **believe**, **conclude**, **know** and **prefer** are rarely continuous.

items.text: We**’re considering** a move to Lisbon.
I **know** what you mean.

blocks.text: Some verbs **do** the action they name: saying ‘I promise’ is the promise. These performatives usually take the present simple.

items.text: I **promise** I’ll be back by ten.
We **advise** all passengers to keep their bags with them.

blocks.text: In negative sentences some of them (**apologise**, **deny**, **guarantee**, **promise**, **suggest**) mean much the same in either form, and a modal makes a performative more polite or tentative:

items.text: I **don’t deny** / I**’m not denying** that it was my idea.
I **would suggest** leaving a little earlier.

blocks.text: Ask whether the verb describes a **state** (how things are) or an **action** (something someone is doing). States take the present simple; a few, like **love** or **look**, can be continuous for a temporary situation.

exercises.instruction: Use the present continuous if you can; otherwise the present simple.

items.text: These boots {{don’t fit|do not fit}} me any more — my feet must have grown.
Why {{are you measuring}} the window? Are you buying new curtains?
The living room {{measures}} about five metres by four.
I {{’m having|am having}} lunch with a client, so I can’t talk now.
items.note: **have** = eat: an action, so it can be continuous.

items.text: Your idea {{sounds}} great to me.
The panel {{consists of}} three judges and a chairman.

exercises.instruction: Choose the better form.

items.text: Quiet, please — I {{’m thinking}} about what to say.
I {{think}} you’re right about the hotel.
Her family {{owns}} a small vineyard in Portugal.
The doctor {{is seeing}} a patient at the moment.
I {{see}} what you mean now.

exercises.instruction: Each pair uses the same verb. Present continuous or present simple?

items.text: The assistant {{is weighing|’s weighing}} the cheese for me.
This suitcase {{weighs}} over twenty kilos!
We {{’re expecting|are expecting}} a delivery this morning.
I {{expect}} you’re tired after the flight.
How {{are you feeling|do you feel}} today?
I {{feel}} that we should wait a little longer.

blocks.text: Thoughts that are just starting can be continuous (**I’m beginning to regret**…, **we’re considering**…). Verbs that perform an action — **promise**, **apologise**, **advise** — take the present simple.

exercises.instruction: Choose the more likely form.

items.text: I {{promise}} I won’t tell anyone.
We {{’re considering}} selling the car.
I {{know}} the answer to that one.
We {{advise}} customers to keep their receipts.
I {{believe}} you.
I {{apologise}} for the delay.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the verbs in brackets.

items.text: I {{suggest}} we leave before the traffic gets bad.
He {{’s considering|is considering}} a complete change of career.
I {{prefer}} trains to planes.
We {{would advise}} you to book early.
items.note: A modal makes the advice more polite.

items.text: I {{don’t deny|’m not denying|do not deny|am not denying}} that I made a mistake.

exercises.instruction: What does each speaker do by saying it?
pairs: I promise to call you tonight.
I warn you, the dog bites.

exercises.instruction: Choose the more likely form in each place.

items.text:
Dear Leo,

Thanks for your message, and I {{apologise|’m apologising}} for not writing sooner. You were right, and I {{admit|’m admitting}} that the first month was hard. I {{’m now realising|now realise}} how much there is to learn, so I {{’m considering|consider}} evening classes in accounting. My manager {{seems|is seeming}} pleased so far, and the office {{has|is having}} a view of the river.

I {{promise|’m promising}} to visit in the spring.

Love, Nina

blocks.text: Verbs that perform the action by saying them — *apologise, admit, promise* — are usually simple. *Realise* and *consider* can be continuous when the meaning is a process going on now.

units.title: Using present continuous and present simple
units.subtitle: Stories, news, headlines and habits

blocks.text: In informal stories and jokes we often use present tenses to make events feel as if they are happening now. The **main events** follow each other in the present simple; **longer background** actions are in the present continuous.

items.text: So I**’m sitting** on the train, minding my own business, and this woman **gets** on and **sits** right on my newspaper …
A penguin **walks** into a café. The waiter**’s cleaning** a glass and **doesn’t** even **look** up …

blocks.text: The present simple can also highlight a sudden event after past tenses, often with **suddenly** or **all of a sudden**:

items.text: I was cycling home when **all of a sudden** a fox **runs** out in front of me.

blocks.text: Sports and other live commentaries describe actions as they happen: quick actions in the present simple, longer ones in the present continuous.

items.text: Okafor **takes** it down the left, **beats** one defender … and the crowd**’s going** wild!

blocks.text: To introduce news we have heard or read, we use the present simple in phrases such as **I hear**, **I gather**, **I see**, **I understand**, **they say**, **it says (here)**, **(someone) tells me**, **(someone) says**. Past tenses are possible too (**Kim said**, **I heard**).

items.text: **I gather** you’ve found a new flat.
Lena **tells me** you’re learning Japanese.
**It says here** that the bridge will be closed all summer.

blocks.text: News headlines use the present simple for events that have just happened, and so do summaries of books, films and plays.

items.text: STORM **CLOSES** CITY AIRPORT
In the second chapter, the detective **finds** a letter hidden in a piano.
In the film, Ruiz **plays** a retired pilot who **returns** for one last job.

blocks.text: With **always**, **constantly**, **continually** and **forever**, the present continuous shows that something happens so often that it is typical of someone — often with irritation. The past continuous works the same way.

items.text: You**’re always leaving** the lights on!
Grandad **was forever telling** the same three jokes.

blocks.text: The present continuous also describes what we are regularly doing at a certain time:

items.text: Don’t call at seven — we**’re** usually **eating** then.

blocks.text: Main events in order: **present simple**. The background that is going on around them: **present continuous**.

exercises.instruction: Present simple or present continuous? Use the verbs in brackets.

items.text: So I’m standing at the bus stop when this man {{walks}} up to me and {{asks}} for my umbrella.
It {{’s pouring|is pouring}} with rain, and everyone {{’s hurrying|is hurrying}} home.
Okafor {{takes}} the ball down the left and {{crosses}} it into the box.
The fans {{’re singing|are singing}} — they {{’re enjoying|are enjoying}} every minute of this.
I was walking home last night when all of a sudden a fox {{runs}} across the road.

exercises.instruction: Choose the form a storyteller or commentator would use.

items.text: A man {{walks}} into a library and asks for a book about paranoia.
The librarian {{’s reading}} a magazine and doesn’t look up.
Then she {{whispers}}: ‘It’s right behind you.’
And Mendes {{scores}}! What a goal!
Both teams {{are playing}} with real energy this afternoon.

exercises.instruction: Put the words in order.

items.answer: So this man walks into a shop.

exercises.instruction: Complete the story. Use the present simple or the present continuous of the verbs in brackets.

items.text: So this woman {{walks}} (walk) into a café. It {{’s pouring|is pouring}} (pour) outside, and she {{’s carrying|is carrying}} (carry) a huge red umbrella. She {{leaves}} (leave) it by the door and {{orders}} (order) a coffee. Ten minutes later a man in a grey coat {{picks}} (pick) it up and {{walks}} (walk) out.

exercises.instruction: Complete the email. Use the present simple or the present continuous of the verbs in brackets.

items.text:
Hi all,

Rita from head office {{says}} (say) that the move to the new building is going ahead. She {{tells|’s telling|is telling}} (tell) me that we {{’re moving|are moving}} (move) in March, and the board {{wants}} (want) everyone to clear their desks by the end of February. I {{hear}} (hear) the canteen there is excellent.

Sam

blocks.text: To pass on news we often use *say, tell, hear* in the present simple — and sometimes *tell* in the present continuous.
**I hear**, **I gather**, **I see**, **I understand**, **they say**, **it says**, **(someone) tells me** — present simple, even though the news reached us earlier.

exercises.instruction: Complete each sentence with a phrase for passing on news.

items.text: {{I hear|I gather|I understand}} you’re moving to Canada.
Marco {{tells me}} the meeting has been cancelled.
{{It says here|It says}} that the museum is free on Sundays.
{{They say}} it’s going to be a cold winter.
{{I see}} the price of petrol has gone up again.

exercises.instruction: Choose the natural phrase.

items.text: {{I gather}} you two have met before.
Lena {{tells me}} you speak Japanese.
{{I hear}} the new café on the corner is excellent.
{{It says}} in the guide that the castle closes at five.

blocks.text: **always / constantly / continually / forever** + present continuous: something typical of a person, often annoying. The past continuous works the same way for the past.

exercises.instruction: Use the words in brackets and the present or past continuous.

items.text: You {{’re always losing|are always losing}} your keys!
My neighbour {{’s constantly complaining|is constantly complaining}} about the noise.
They {{’re forever arguing|are forever arguing}} about money.
Jo {{’s always helping|is always helping}} other people — she’s so kind.
When we shared a flat, he {{was always borrowing}} my bike.

exercises.instruction: Make a complaint or a comment.

items.answer: They were forever asking for money.

exercises.instruction: Expand one set of notes to finish each reply.
exercises.example:
**A** Where are my keys again?
**B** You’re **forever losing your keys**.

items.text:
**A** Sorry — one quick message, then I’m all yours.
**B** You’re {{constantly checking your phone|constantly checking the phone}}.

**A** Can I take yours? Mine’s flat.
**B** You’re {{always borrowing my charger}}.
items.note: After *always* the verb is in the **-ing** form.

items.text:
**A** Wait — let me just finish my point!
**B** You’re {{continually interrupting me}}.

**A** Let’s go to the beach tomorrow instead.
**B** You’re {{forever changing our plans|forever changing the plans}}.

blocks.text: Headlines and plot summaries: **present simple**. What we are usually doing at a certain time: **present continuous** (**At eight I’m usually driving to work**).

exercises.instruction: Present simple or present continuous?

items.text: Mayor {{resigns}} after funding scandal
In chapter one, the detective {{finds}} a letter hidden in a piano.
In the film, Ruiz {{plays}} a retired pilot.
Don’t ring at eight — we {{’re usually eating|are usually eating}} then.
At half past eight I {{’m normally taking|am normally taking}} the kids to school.

exercises.instruction: Choose the better form.

items.text: Earthquake {{hits}} northern Chile
In the novel, the hero {{loses}} everything in the first chapter.
Call me later — at six I’m usually {{cooking}}.
Our team {{beats}} the champions in the last minute

units.title: Past simple and present perfect
units.subtitle: Finished time, since, time clauses and news

blocks.text: With **this morning / week / month** and **today** we use the past simple if we see the period as **finished**, and the present perfect if it **includes now**.

items.text: I **didn’t check** my email this morning. *(said in the evening: the morning is over)*
I **haven’t checked** my email this morning. *(said at eleven: there’s still time)*

blocks.text: In a sentence with **since**, the since-clause usually has the past simple (a point in the past) and the main clause the present perfect.

items.text: Prices **have risen** sharply *since* the new tax **came** in.
She **hasn’t driven** *since* she **had** the accident.

blocks.text: If both situations go on until now, both clauses take the present perfect:

items.text: **Have** you **made** any friends *since* you**’ve lived** here?

blocks.text: After **after**, **when**, **until**, **as soon as**, **once**, **by the time** and **the minute / second / moment**, the past simple refers to finished past events, and the present perfect to events in the **future**.

items.text: *Once* she **read** the letter, she burst into tears. *(past)*
*Once* you**’ve read** the instructions, you’ll find it easy. *(future)*
I’ll call you *the minute* I**’ve landed**. *(future)*

blocks.text: The past perfect (**after she had left**) and the present simple (**after he leaves**) are also possible with the same meanings.
News reports often **introduce** a recent event with the present perfect and then give the **details** in the past simple.

items.text: A missing climber **has been found** alive in the Alps. Rescuers **reached** him early on Tuesday.

blocks.text: After **It / This / That is** or **will be the first time**, we use the present perfect. After **It was the first time**, we use the past perfect.

items.text: *This is the first time* I**’ve tried** sushi.
*It will be the first time* the club **has reached** a final.
*It was the first time* she**’d flown** alone.

blocks.text: Is the period over when you speak? Over: **past simple**. Still going: **present perfect**.

exercises.instruction: Present perfect or past simple? Mind the time in brackets.

items.text: (11 a.m.) I {{haven’t had|have not had}} any coffee this morning — no wonder I’m tired.
(9 p.m.) I {{didn’t have|did not have}} time for breakfast this morning.
I {{’ve sent|have sent}} thirty emails today, and it’s only lunchtime.
(5 p.m.) I {{overslept}} this morning, so I missed the first meeting.
It’s only the 20th and we {{’ve spent|have spent}} the whole budget for this month.

exercises.instruction: Choose the better form.

items.text: (10 a.m.) I {{haven’t seen}} Tom this morning.
(Evening) I {{didn’t see}} Tom this morning — was he ill?
(Thursday) It {{’s been}} a busy week so far.
(Monday) It {{was}} a lovely weekend.

blocks.text: Since + a point in the past: **past simple**; the main clause: **present perfect**. If both situations continue until now, both are in the present perfect.

exercises.instruction: Present perfect or past simple? Use the verbs in brackets.

items.text: Prices {{have risen|’ve risen}} sharply since the new tax {{came}} in.
She {{hasn’t driven|has not driven}} since she {{had}} the accident.
A lot {{has changed|’s changed}} since I last {{wrote}} to you.
Since he {{started}} running, he {{’s felt|has felt}} much healthier.
Have you {{made}} any friends since you {{’ve lived|have lived}} here?
items.note: You still live here, so **since you’ve lived**.

exercises.instruction: Choose the better form.

items.text: Since I {{moved}} here, I’ve made lots of friends.
Since I {{’ve worked}} from home, I’ve saved a fortune on travel.
He’s been much happier since he {{changed}} jobs.

blocks.text: After **when, once, as soon as, until, the minute**…: past simple for the **past**, present perfect for the **future**.

exercises.instruction: Past or future? Choose the form.

items.text: Once you {{’ve read}} the instructions, you’ll find it easy.
I’ll call you the minute I {{’ve landed}}.
The minute I {{landed}}, I switched on my phone.
We can’t leave until everyone {{has paid}}.
By the time we {{got}} there, the film had started.

exercises.instruction: Present perfect or past simple?

items.text: As soon as I {{’ve finished|have finished}} this report, I’ll join you.
After he {{left}} university, he travelled for a year.
When you {{’ve found|have found}} a seat, please wait for the announcement.
I recognised her the moment she {{spoke}}.

exercises.instruction: One sentence in each pair is wrong. Correct the verb in it; keep ✓ for the right one.

items.text:
a  Once you {{signed => ’ve signed|have signed|sign}} the form, you can’t cancel the order.
b  Once she {{signed}}, the deal was done.

a  The minute I {{landed}}, I switched my phone back on.
b  I’ll text you the minute I {{landed => land|’ve landed|have landed}}.

a  We can’t leave until everyone {{paid => has paid|’s paid|pays}}.
b  We waited until everyone {{had paid}}.

blocks.text: News: introduce with the **present perfect**, give details in the **past simple**. **It’s / It will be the first time** + present perfect; **It was the first time** + past perfect.

exercises.instruction: Use the verbs in brackets in the right tense.

items.text: A missing climber {{has been found|’s been found}} alive. Rescuers {{reached}} him early on Tuesday.
The company {{has announced|’s announced}} record profits. Sales {{rose}} by 12% last year.
This is the first time I {{’ve eaten|have eaten}} octopus.
It will be the first time the club {{has played|’s played}} in a final.
It was the first time she {{’d flown|had flown}} alone.

exercises.instruction: Choose the better form.

items.text: This is the first time I {{’ve been}} to Rome.
It was the first time we {{’d met}}.
Police {{have arrested}} two men after a robbery in the city centre.
The robbery {{happened}} at about three in the morning.

exercises.instruction: Correct the verbs in italics where they are wrong.

items.text: Maria Costa {{has won}} the National Bread Award. It’s the first time a baker from our town {{won => has won|’s won}} it. Maria {{opened}} her bakery in 2015, and she {{has made => made}} her first sourdough loaf the same week. “I {{’ve never been}} so surprised,” she told us.
